cards.q: What is a photon?
cards.a: A discrete packet (quantum) of electromagnetic energy. Its energy depends on its frequency: \(E = hf\).

cards.q: Write the energy of a photon in terms of its wavelength.
cards.a: \(E = \frac{hc}{\lambda}\)
cards.why: It follows from \(E = hf\) and \(c = f\lambda\). A shorter wavelength means a more energetic photon.

cards.q: Calculate the energy of a photon of wavelength 500 nm. (\(h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34}\ \text{J s}\), \(c = 3.00 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m s}^{-1}\))
cards.a: \(4.0 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{J}\)

cards.q: State the unit of the Planck constant.
cards.a: J s (joule second).
cards.why: From \(E = hf\): \(h = \frac{E}{f}\), a joule divided by a hertz.

cards.q: Define the electronvolt.
cards.a: The energy gained by an electron accelerated through a potential difference of 1 volt. \(1\ \text{eV} = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{J}\).

cards.q: Convert 2.5 eV into joules.
cards.a: \(4.0 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{J}\)
steps: To go from eV to J, multiply by \(1.60 \times 10^{-19}\).

cards.q: Convert \(3.2 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{J}\) into electronvolts.
cards.a: 2.0 eV
steps: To go from J to eV, divide by \(1.60 \times 10^{-19}\).
cards.why: A joule is a huge unit on the atomic scale, so the number in eV is always the much bigger one. Use that to check which way to convert.

cards.q: What is the photoelectric effect?
cards.a: The emission of electrons from the surface of a metal when electromagnetic radiation of high enough frequency falls on it.

cards.q: Define the threshold frequency of a metal.
cards.a: The minimum frequency of electromagnetic radiation that will cause photoelectrons to be emitted from the metal's surface.

cards.q: Define the work function of a metal.
cards.a: The minimum energy needed to remove an electron from the surface of the metal.
cards.why: The word minimum is needed for the mark.

cards.q: In the photoelectric equation \(hf = \phi + E_{k(\text{max})}\), what does each term represent?
cards.a: \(hf\): the energy of one photon. \(\phi\): the work function of the metal. \(E_{k(\text{max})}\): the maximum kinetic energy of an emitted photoelectron.
cards.why: It is conservation of energy for one photon and one electron.

cards.q: Why does the photoelectric equation give the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons, and not the energy of all of them?
cards.a: The work function is the least energy needed to escape. Electrons below the surface need more than this to get out, so they leave with less kinetic energy.

cards.q: How is the threshold frequency \(f_{0}\) of a metal related to its work function \(\phi\)?
cards.why: At the threshold frequency a photon has just enough energy to free an electron, with no kinetic energy left over.

cards.q: Light of frequency \(7.0 \times 10^{14}\ \text{Hz}\) falls on a metal of work function \(3.7 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{J}\). Calculate the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons. (\(h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34}\ \text{J s}\))
cards.a: \(9.4 \times 10^{-20}\ \text{J}\)

cards.q: A metal has a work function of 2.3 eV. Calculate its threshold frequency. (\(h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34}\ \text{J s}\), \(e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{C}\))
cards.a: \(5.6 \times 10^{14}\ \text{Hz}\)
steps: Convert the work function to joules: \(2.3 \times 1.60 \times 10^{-19} = 3.68 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{J}\).
cards.why: The energy must be in joules before it is used with the Planck constant.

cards.q: Explain, using the photon model, why no photoelectrons are emitted below the threshold frequency, however bright the light.
cards.a: Each electron is freed by a single photon, and below the threshold no single photon has enough energy.
marks: Light arrives as photons, each of energy \(hf\).
One photon is absorbed by one electron.
An electron escapes only if the photon's energy is at least the work function.
Below the threshold frequency \(hf\) is less than the work function, so no electron can escape.
Brighter light means more photons per second, not more energy per photon.

cards.q: Light above the threshold frequency falls on a metal. Its intensity is increased, with the frequency unchanged. What happens to the photoelectrons?
cards.a: More electrons are emitted each second, but their maximum kinetic energy does not change.
cards.why: Intensity sets the number of photons arriving each second. The energy of each photon depends only on frequency.

cards.q: A student says: "Brighter light gives the photoelectrons more kinetic energy." Correct this.
cards.a: The maximum kinetic energy depends on the frequency of the light, not its brightness. Brighter light of the same frequency releases more electrons, each with the same maximum energy.

cards.q: Give two observations about the photoelectric effect that the wave model of light cannot explain.
cards.a: There is a threshold frequency, below which no electrons are emitted whatever the intensity. And emission is immediate, even in very dim light: on the wave model energy would build up gradually.

cards.q: What is the stopping potential, and how is it related to the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons?
cards.a: The potential difference needed to stop the most energetic photoelectrons. \(eV_{s} = E_{k(\text{max})}\).

cards.q: Photoelectrons are emitted with a maximum kinetic energy of \(9.4 \times 10^{-20}\ \text{J}\). Calculate the stopping potential. (\(e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{C}\))
cards.a: 0.59 V

cards.q: A graph is plotted of the maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons against the frequency of the light. What do its gradient and its two intercepts represent?
cards.a: Gradient: the Planck constant \(h\). Intercept on the frequency axis: the threshold frequency. Intercept on the energy axis: \(-\phi\), the work function with a minus sign.

cards.q: What is meant by the ground state of an atom?
cards.a: The lowest energy state of the atom, with its electrons in the lowest energy levels available.

cards.q: What is excitation of an atom?
cards.a: An electron in the atom moves to a higher energy level by absorbing energy.

cards.q: What is ionisation of an atom?
cards.a: An electron is removed from the atom altogether, leaving a positive ion.

cards.q: An atom can be excited by absorbing a photon or by a collision with an electron. How do the energy requirements differ?
cards.a: A photon must have exactly the energy difference between two levels, because it is absorbed whole. A colliding electron needs at least that energy: it gives up the amount required and keeps the rest as kinetic energy.

cards.q: Explain how a fluorescent tube produces visible light.
cards.a: Mercury atoms emit ultraviolet photons, and the tube's coating converts them to visible light.
marks: Electrons are accelerated through the tube and collide with mercury atoms.
The collisions excite (or ionise) the mercury atoms.
The atoms de-excite, emitting photons, mostly ultraviolet.
The coating on the inside of the tube absorbs the ultraviolet photons, exciting its atoms.
These atoms de-excite in smaller steps, emitting photons of lower energy: visible light.

cards.q: An electron drops from an energy level \(E_{1}\) to a lower level \(E_{2}\). Write the equation for the frequency of the photon emitted.
cards.why: The photon carries away exactly the energy the atom loses.

cards.q: An electron in a hydrogen atom drops from the −1.5 eV level to the −3.4 eV level. Calculate the frequency of the photon emitted. (\(h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34}\ \text{J s}\), \(e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{C}\))
cards.a: \(4.6 \times 10^{14}\ \text{Hz}\)

cards.q: A photon is emitted in a transition between two energy levels \(3.04 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{J}\) apart. Calculate its wavelength. (\(h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34}\ \text{J s}\), \(c = 3.00 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m s}^{-1}\))
cards.a: \(6.5 \times 10^{-7}\ \text{m}\) (650 nm, red light)

cards.q: Explain how line spectra provide evidence that atoms have discrete energy levels.
cards.a: Only certain photon energies appear, so only certain energy changes are possible.
marks: A line spectrum contains only certain wavelengths (frequencies).
Each line corresponds to photons of one particular energy.
A photon is emitted when an electron moves between two energy levels, with energy equal to the difference between them.
Only certain photon energies means only certain energy differences, so the levels must be discrete.

cards.q: What is the difference between an emission line spectrum and an absorption line spectrum?
cards.a: An emission spectrum is bright lines on a dark background, from atoms emitting photons as electrons drop to lower levels. An absorption spectrum is dark lines on a continuous spectrum, where atoms have absorbed photons of exactly the right energies.
cards.why: For one element the lines are at the same wavelengths in both.

cards.q: Why are the energy levels of an atom given negative values?
cards.a: Zero energy is taken to be an electron that is just free of the atom. A bound electron has less energy than that, so its energy is negative: energy must be supplied to remove it.

cards.q: State one piece of evidence that light behaves as a particle, and one that electrons behave as waves.
cards.a: Light as a particle: the photoelectric effect. Electrons as waves: electron diffraction.

cards.q: Which behaviours of light need the wave model, and which need the photon model?
cards.a: Wave model: diffraction, interference and polarisation. Photon model: the photoelectric effect and line spectra.
cards.why: Neither model alone explains everything light does.

cards.q: Write the de Broglie equation, and say what each symbol means.
cards.a: \(\lambda = \frac{h}{mv}\), where \(\lambda\) is the de Broglie wavelength of the particle, \(h\) the Planck constant and \(mv\) the particle's momentum.

cards.q: Calculate the de Broglie wavelength of an electron moving at \(2.0 \times 10^{6}\ \text{m s}^{-1}\). (\(h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34}\ \text{J s}\), \(m_{e} = 9.11 \times 10^{-31}\ \text{kg}\))
cards.a: \(3.6 \times 10^{-10}\ \text{m}\)
cards.why: This is about the spacing of atoms in a crystal, which is why crystals diffract electrons.

cards.q: An electron is accelerated from rest through a potential difference of 150 V. Calculate its de Broglie wavelength. (\(h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34}\ \text{J s}\), \(m_{e} = 9.11 \times 10^{-31}\ \text{kg}\), \(e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{C}\))
cards.a: \(1.0 \times 10^{-10}\ \text{m}\)

cards.q: In an electron diffraction tube, the accelerating potential difference is increased. Explain what happens to the diffraction rings.
cards.a: The rings get smaller (closer together).
marks: A larger potential difference gives the electrons more kinetic energy, so more momentum.
By \(\lambda = \frac{h}{mv}\), a larger momentum means a shorter de Broglie wavelength.
A shorter wavelength is diffracted through smaller angles, so the rings have smaller diameters.

cards.q: Why is a thin crystal, such as graphite, used to show electron diffraction?
cards.a: The spacing between its atoms is about the same as the de Broglie wavelength of the electrons, so the gaps between atoms diffract them noticeably.

cards.q: A proton and an electron travel at the same speed. Which has the longer de Broglie wavelength, and why?
cards.a: The electron. It has a much smaller mass, so a much smaller momentum, and \(\lambda = \frac{h}{mv}\).

cards.q: How does a new idea in physics, such as wave–particle duality, come to be accepted?
cards.a: It is published, evaluated by other scientists through peer review, and tested by experiments that others can repeat. It is accepted once it has been validated by the scientific community.
